Issued at 300 AM EDT Fri Oct 16 2026

Today-Tonight...A cold front moves into the Southeast U.S. today 
pushing high pressure north of the area farther east. Winds weaken
and will be somewhat variable today, with the east coast sea 
breeze developing into the afternoon and winds along the coast 
becoming onshore and increasing to 5-10 mph. Moisture continues to
build northward across the area with PW values around 2.0" across
the area today. This will lead to greater rain chances today 
(around 50-70%), with scattered showers and storms developing 
primarily into the afternoon and evening. However isolated to 
scattered coastal showers will be possible this morning. Temps 
remain relatively warm aloft (around -6C at 500mb), but there will
be some pockets of drier air aloft, with DCAPE values around 
500-800 J/kg that may still lead to a few stronger storms today. 
Main threats will be frequent lightning strikes, strong wind gusts
to 40-45 mph and heavy downpours. Slow storm motion toward the 
N-NE and moist airmass in place may lead to locally heavy rainfall
of 2-4 inches from any storms or heavier showers. This may lead 
to mostly minor flooding, but with saturated ground conditions 
can't completely rule out an isolated instance of flash flooding. 
A Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 4) for excessive rainfall exits across
much of the area today. 

Temperatures will be above normal, ranging from the upper 80s along 
the coast to upper 80s/low 90s inland. More humid conditions today 
will also produce peak heat index values around 98-102F. Warm and 
muggy conditions continue overnight, with lows in the low to mid 
70s. 

Saturday-Thursday...Cold front pushes southward through the area 
Saturday, with north-northeast winds becoming breezy to windy into 
the afternoon. Sustained winds look to increase to 15-20 mph inland 
and up to 20-25 mph along the coast, with gusts up to 30-35 mph. 
While a Wind Advisory for portions of the coast can't be completely 
ruled out for Saturday afternoon, better potential exists along the 
coast into Saturday night and across much of the area Sunday, as 
northeast winds increase further from tightening pressure gradient 
between strong high building in north of the stalled front south of 
the area. Gusts up to 35-40 mph (potentially slightly higher along 
the coast) will be possible. A tight pressure gradient will continue 
through early to middle portion of next week, as cut-off low 
develops a strong area of low pressure offshore of the Mid-Atlantic 
coast, maintaining breezy to windy NE winds across the region. This 
prolonged period of increased onshore flow, will lead to hazardous 
coastal conditions. Rough surf, large breaking waves, and a high 
risk of life-threatening rip currents will be present at all area 
beaches. Entering the water is highly discouraged! Long period 
onshore swells will also likely contribute to moderate beach erosion 
through multiple high tide cycles. 

High coverage of showers and isolated to scattered storms will 
continue into Saturday with the passing front, with highest rain 
chances southeast of the I-4 corridor. As flow veers onshore 
persistent shower bands or storms may still lead to a risk of 
flooding, mainly along the Treasure Coast into Saturday afternoon 
and Saturday night. A Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 4) of excessive 
rainfall persists for this region tomorrow. Drier air works in 
behind the front lowering PW values below 1.5" by Sunday, but the 
strong NE breeze will still generate rounds of scattered onshore 
moving showers Sunday and through much of next week, with greatest 
potential for rain across the coastal counties. A few storms pushing 
onshore will also be possible, mainly south of the Cape. 

It will turn cooler behind the front into the weekend with highs 
falling as low as the the mid 70s to low 80s by Sunday and Monday, 
and then some gradual warming is forecast. Overnight lows drop 
into the 60s, but along the immediate coast the stronger NE breeze
may keep min temps in the 70s.
